newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, lawmakers map foreign policy strategy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, lawmakers map foreign policy strategy.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and his advisers held a foreign policy brainstorming session with members of Congress on Wednesday night as Clinton pressed for Senate approval of a chemical weapons treaty.

The informal closed-door discussion took place over dinner at Blair House, an official government guest residence across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, and brought Clinton together with three dozen leading lawmakers of both parties.

"It was a good opportunity as the president as hoped, not only for him and members of his administration to present some ideas and to talk about the administration's views, but to hear some ideas that the congressmen and senators had," White House spokesman David Johnson said.

Among topics talked over at the session were the pending enlargement of NATO, engagement with China, the international fight against terrorism and narcotics trafficking, efforts to expand world trade, and U.S-led peacekeeping in Bosnia.
"This was not focused on a particular topic or a particular decision point as much as it was on how to work together on a bipartisan foreign policy," Johnson said.
Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican invited to the session, said it was "a valuable meeting and I think we ought to do more of them."
Clinton and Vice President Al Gore "were reaching out to all of us on a bipartisan basis," said McCain, who added that there was "no arm-twisting."

Administration participants also included Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, Commerce Secretary William Daley and National Security Adviser Samuel Berger.

The nearly four hour meeting occurred at a time when Russia is rankled at NATO plans to expand into former Soviet satellites, the Middle East peace process has stalemated and Clinton's China policy is under fire from House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and others.
But of more immediate concern for Clinton and his team was the fate of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), a treaty that would outlaw poison gas and other chemical weapons.
The accord takes effect on April 29, and the administration argues that the United States will be at a serious disadvantage if it has not ratified the pact by then.

Johnson said Clinton had made a strong pitch for support of the treaty after earlier calling about 10 senators to ask for their votes. Critics say the treaty would not work and expose U.S. chemical companies to outside inspection.
Approval is "very much up in the air at this point," said Berger. "There is some strenuous opposition from some groups."
Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is a leading critic of the accord. He declined to attend the dinner meeting.

Another topic of the high-powered skull session was if and when the Republican Congress will give Democrat Clinton so-called fast-track authority to bring Chile into the North American Free Trade Agreement linking the United States, Mexico and Canada.
The authority would give Clinton the power to conclude a trade agreement with Chile that Congress could vote for or against but would not be able to slow down with amendments.
